stem: A nurse notes that the dressing over a central venous catheter has become loose and no longer fully covers the insertion site. The catheter remains clinically indicated. Which action is most appropriate?

options.A: Perform hand hygiene and replace the loose dressing promptly using aseptic catheter-site care and an appropriate sterile dressing.
options.B: Secure the loose edges with additional tape if the site appears dry, then replace the dressing at the next routine scheduled interval.
options.C: Place a second transparent dressing over the existing loose dressing so the original catheter-site barrier does not have to be disturbed.
options.D: Stop using the catheter and arrange replacement at a new insertion site before changing the loose dressing, even when no catheter complication is present.

rationale: CDC guidance states that an intravascular catheter-site dressing should be replaced when it becomes damp, loosened, or visibly soiled. CDC also recommends hand hygiene before and after dressing an intravascular catheter and maintaining aseptic technique for catheter care. Therefore A is correct. Taping or covering over a compromised dressing does not restore the recommended catheter-site dressing change, and a loose dressing by itself is not a CDC indication to remove an otherwise clinically indicated central venous catheter.
educational_objective: When a central-line dressing becomes loose, promptly replace it using hand hygiene, aseptic catheter-site care, and an appropriate sterile dressing rather than patching the compromised barrier or removing an otherwise needed catheter.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Guidelines for the Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections — Summary of Recommendations
source_version_date: Current CDC Infection Control web guidance accessed 2026-08-25
source_locator: Hand Hygiene and Aseptic Technique, Recommendations 1–2: perform hand hygiene before and after dressing an intravascular catheter and maintain aseptic technique for catheter care. Catheter Site Dressing Regimens, Recommendations 1 and 3: cover the site with sterile gauze or a sterile transparent semipermeable dressing and replace the catheter-site dressing if it becomes damp, loosened, or visibly soiled.
source_claim_supported: A loose central-line dressing should be replaced promptly with appropriate sterile dressing care using hand hygiene and aseptic technique.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p. 38: access and/or maintain central venous access devices; monitor intravenous infusion and maintain site.
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — central venous catheter dressing integrity and maintenance
correction_summary: Rebuilt the distractors to eliminate absolute-word cueing and made all alternatives realistic catheter-maintenance choices. The corrected item uses direct CDC dressing-change and aseptic-care recommendations and tightens the NCLEX mapping to Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, which explicitly includes central venous access-device maintenance.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Central venous access device — compromised dressing integrity
audit_findings.stem: PASS — explicitly states a loose dressing, incomplete site coverage, and ongoing catheter indication without introducing an infection diagnosis.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly matches CDC recommendations for loose dressings, hand hygiene, aseptic technique, and sterile site coverage; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — additional tape may appear practical, but CDC directs replacement when the dressing is loosened rather than waiting for the routine interval.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — covering over the compromised dressing does not perform the recommended replacement and leaves the original barrier problem unresolved.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — catheter removal can be appropriate for specific indications, but looseness of the dressing alone calls for dressing replacement rather than automatic line replacement.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only option that fully restores dressing integrity using the directly recommended maintenance steps.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B and C patch rather than replace the loosened dressing; D unnecessarily replaces a still-indicated catheter without another complication.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — the keyed answer is comparable in length and specificity to the distractors and no keyed-only absolute wording remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies explicitly includes central venous access-device maintenance.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether taping, overlaying, or replacing the catheter itself could be equally appropriate; CDC directly requires dressing replacement for looseness while separately reserving catheter removal for clinical indications, leaving A uniquely best.
